x: Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) is the reddish-brown gas with a choking smell. Chlorine is greenish-yellow, fluorine pale yellow and SO₂ colourless.
t: Recall the colour of each gas.

x: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin, and it has no colour or smell, so it is the silent killer.
t: Recall why CO is dangerous.

x: Hydrogen comes from electrolysis of water, oxygen from heating KMnO₄ or KClO₃, chlorine from electrolysis of brine and H₂S from FeS with dilute HCl, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the preparation of each gas.

x: Hydrogen is used in ammonia synthesis and rocket fuel, chlorine in water purification and PVC, CO₂ in soft drinks and extinguishers, and N₂O as an anaesthetic, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the use of each gas.

x: Option C is incorrect: ground-level ozone is a smog pollutant that harms lungs and plants. High in the stratosphere ozone shields us from UV, and CFCs deplete it.
t: Discriminate ground-level ozone (harmful) from stratospheric ozone (protective).

x: Both are true and R explains A: CO locks onto haemoglobin as a stable complex, so less haemoglobin is free to carry oxygen.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the N≡N triple bond is very strong, so nitrogen barely reacts at room temperature.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All three are correct: CO₂ (44) and H₂S (34) are heavier than air (about 29), while ammonia (17) is lighter.
t: Compare each molar mass with air's 29.

x: Three are used in rockets: hydrogen as fuel, and oxygen and nitrous oxide as oxidisers. Nitrogen is inert and is not a propellant.
t: Recall rocket fuels and oxidisers.

x: Hydrogen is H₂, oxygen O₂, nitrogen N₂ and carbon dioxide CO₂, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the formulas of common gases.

x: All three are correct: hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen are all colourless and odourless.
t: Recall the physical properties of gases.

x: Chlorine is greenish-yellow with a choking smell, ammonia colourless and sharp, SO₂ colourless and suffocating, and CO colourless and odourless, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Recall the colour and smell of each gas.

x: Both are true: carbon dioxide is colourless and odourless.
t: Recall the properties of CO₂.

x: H₂S smells of rotten eggs, NO₂ is reddish-brown, N₂O is sweet-smelling laughing gas and ozone is pale blue with a sharp smell, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii.
t: Recall the colour and smell of each gas.

x: Both are true: phosphine (PH₃) is colourless with a rotten-fish smell, and fluorine (F₂) is pale yellow with an irritating smell.
t: Recall the colour and smell of each gas.

x: All four are correct: hydrogen is the lightest gas, burns with a pale blue flame, is non-toxic, and can suffocate by displacing oxygen at high levels.
t: Recall the properties of hydrogen.

x: Both are true: oxygen supports burning and is paramagnetic, and it is non-toxic and essential for respiration.
t: Recall the properties of oxygen.

x: All four are correct: nitrogen is inert, unreactive and a non-toxic asphyxiant, and chlorine (71) is denser than air.
t: Recall the properties of nitrogen and chlorine.

x: Chlorine is a toxic strong oxidiser, ammonia is basic and very soluble, SO₂ is an acidic irritant oxide and NO₂ is an acidic toxic oxidiser, giving a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.
t: Recall the chemical nature of each gas.

x: Both are true: H₂S is extremely toxic and, at high levels, paralyses the sense of smell, so its warning odour vanishes.
t: Recall why H₂S is dangerous.

x: Carbon monoxide is highly toxic. The other options describe chlorine (oxidiser), carbon dioxide (asphyxiant at high level) and NO₂ (acidic oxidiser).
t: Discriminate CO from CO₂.

x: Ozone is a powerful oxidising agent, used to disinfect water. Basic and soluble describes ammonia, and inert describes nitrogen.
t: Recall the chemical nature of ozone.

x: All four are correct: hydrogen comes from water and hydrocarbons, oxygen from air (21%) and water, nitrogen from air (78%) and chlorine from chlorides in sea water.
t: Recall the natural source of each gas.

x: Hydrogen is made from zinc and dilute H₂SO₄, oxygen by fractional distillation of liquid air, nitrogen by heating NH₄NO₂ and chlorine from MnO₂ with conc. HCl, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the lab and industrial preparation of each gas.

x: Both are given as true: hydrogen is made industrially by steam reforming of methane, and no natural source is listed for ammonia.
t: Recall the preparation of hydrogen.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the Haber process combines nitrogen and hydrogen over an iron catalyst to make ammonia.
t: Check whether R is the method in A.

x: Both are true: ammonia is made in the lab by heating NH₄Cl with Ca(OH)₂, and SO₂ by burning sulphur.
t: Recall the lab preparation of each gas.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: being an acidic oxide is a property, not why volcanoes and fossil fuels release SO₂.
t: Check whether R is a source or only a property.

x: All four are correct: SO₂ comes from copper with conc. H₂SO₄ or roasting FeS₂, CO from formic acid with conc. H₂SO₄, and CO₂ from heating carbonates.
t: Recall the preparation of each gas.

x: Both are true: carbon monoxide comes from incomplete burning, and CO₂ is made in the lab from CaCO₃ and dilute HCl.
t: Recall the source and preparation of carbon oxides.

x: Both are true and R explains A: ammonia's toxicity shows as irritation of the eyes and airways.
t: Check whether R is the effect behind A.

x: All seven are correct: nitrogen is got from liquid air, CO₂ comes from respiration, volcanoes and burning, and H₂S from natural gas, petroleum and volcanoes.
t: Recall the sources of each gas.

x: All seven are correct: hydrogen is used to harden oils, in fuel cells and as a reducer, and oxygen in respiration, steelmaking, welding and hospitals.
t: Recall the uses of hydrogen and oxygen.

x: All four are nitrogen uses: making fertiliser via ammonia, inert atmospheres, food packaging and liquid-nitrogen cryogenics.
t: Recall the uses of nitrogen.

x: Chlorine is used for bleaching, disinfecting and making HCl, while ammonia is used for fertilisers such as urea, giving a-ii, b-ii, c-ii, d-i.
t: Discriminate chlorine uses from ammonia uses.

x: Ammonia is used to make nitric acid, in refrigeration and in cleaners, and SO₂ as a bleaching agent. With List-I repeating, the code pairs in order, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall that the code pairs items in order when List-I repeats.

x: SO₂ is used as a preservative, to make sulphuric acid and as a refrigerant, while CO reduces ores in metallurgy, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the uses of SO₂ and CO.

x: CO extracts iron from its ore, CO₂ is used by plants in photosynthesis, and ozone purifies water and bleaches, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the uses of carbon oxides and ozone.

x: Ozone kills microbes and is used as a disinfectant. Refrigeration and nitric acid use ammonia, and metallurgical reduction uses CO.
t: Recall the use of each gas.

x: Both are true and R explains A: CO₂ traps outgoing infrared heat as a greenhouse gas, so more CO₂ warms the climate.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All four are correct: nitrogen oxides cause acid rain, photochemical smog and breathing problems, and carbon monoxide is an air pollutant.
t: Recall the effects of air pollutants.

x: Both are true: methane is a potent greenhouse gas, and hydrogen sulphide is a toxic pollutant.
t: Recall the effects of methane and H₂S.

x: H₂S oxidises to SO₂, so it adds to acid-rain precursors. Smog comes from nitrogen oxides, warming from CO₂ and UV protection from ozone.
t: Recall the environmental effect of each gas.

x: Both are true and R explains A: hydrogen combines with most elements, which shows how reactive it is.
t: Check whether R is evidence for A.

x: All three are correct: sulphur is a moderately reactive solid, and white phosphorus is so reactive it catches fire in air, so it is kept under water.
t: Recall how reactive non-metals are stored.

x: Carbon is a solid with variable reactivity, diamond is inert and graphite less reactive, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the reactivity of carbon allotropes.

x: Both are true: noble gases are all gases at room temperature, and helium and neon are among them.
t: Recall the noble gases.

x: Both are true: chlorine and fluorine can form toxic compounds, and fluorine is the most reactive non-metal.
t: Recall the reactivity of halogens.

x: Argon is a noble gas in Group 18, making up almost 1% of air. It is not a greenhouse gas or an oxidiser.
t: Recall the noble gases.

x: Both are true: noble gases have full shells and barely react, while oxygen is very reactive and supports burning.
t: Discriminate inert noble gases from reactive oxygen.

x: Noble gases are inert because their outer electron shells are full. They do not oxidise, react or support burning.
t: Recall why noble gases are inert.

x: All four are correct: SO₂ is toxic and causes acid rain, respiratory disease and damage to plants and buildings.
t: Recall the effects of SO₂.

x: At room temperature chlorine is a gas, bromine a liquid and iodine a solid, giving (a)-(i), (b)-(ii), (c)-(iii).
t: Recall that halogens go gas, liquid, solid down the group.

x: Chlorine is highly reactive, second only to fluorine among halogens. Iodine is the least reactive, so options B and C are wrong.
t: Recall that halogen reactivity falls down the group.

x: Option D is incorrect: bromine is a liquid at room temperature, the only liquid non-metal. It is reactive.
t: Recall bromine as the liquid non-metal.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: iodine is least reactive because its large atom holds an extra electron weakly; being solid is a separate physical fact.
t: Check whether R is a cause or a parallel fact.

x: Hydrogen has the highest calorific value of common fuels, about 1,50,000 kJ/kg, roughly three times that of petrol.
t: Recall hydrogen's calorific value.

x: Grey hydrogen (from natural gas) releases high CO₂, blue captures it for low emissions, green (renewable electrolysis) has zero, and brown/black (coal) very high, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Recall the emissions of each hydrogen colour.

x: Option B is incorrect: hydrogen burns to give only water, with no carbon dioxide. A fuel cell makes electricity and water, and hydrogen burns with a pale blue flame.
t: Recall that hydrogen contains no carbon.

x: Both are true and R explains A: hydrogen must be made using other energy and then stores and moves it, so it is a carrier, not a primary source.
t: Check whether R is the reason for A.

x: Both are true: a fuel cell turns hydrogen and oxygen into electricity and water, so nothing harmful comes out at the point of use.
t: Recall how a fuel cell works.

x: I and II are correct: green hydrogen can replace coking coal in steel, and green ammonia and methanol can carry energy for export. III is false because aviation uses hydrogen-based synthetic fuels, not hydrogen directly.
t: Discriminate direct hydrogen use from synthetic fuels.

x: Steam reforming of natural gas gives grey or blue hydrogen, coal or biomass gasification gives grey or brown, renewable electrolysis gives green, and methane pyrolysis gives turquoise, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
t: Recall the source and colour of each method.

x: Three are fuel or transport uses: fuel-cell vehicles, rocket fuel and blending with CNG. Ammonia for fertiliser is an industrial use.
t: Discriminate transport uses from industrial uses.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: grey hydrogen dominates because natural gas infrastructure is everywhere, not just because it is cheap.
t: Check whether R is a full reason or only a related fact.

x: India's National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023) focuses on green hydrogen made by electrolysis with renewable power.
t: Recall the focus of India's hydrogen mission.

x: Pink or purple hydrogen comes from electrolysis with nuclear power and has near-zero CO₂, and turquoise comes from methane pyrolysis leaving solid carbon and is an emerging route, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the source of each hydrogen colour.

x: Nuclear electrolysis uses water and nuclear power to give pink hydrogen, and biological routes use microbes or algae as emerging green options, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the source of each hydrogen colour.

x: All four are correct: hydrogen is colourless, odourless and tasteless, the lightest element and the least dense gas.
t: Recall the properties of hydrogen.

x: All three are correct: refineries use hydrogen to remove sulphur, it is used to make methanol, and it is a general chemical feedstock.
t: Recall the industrial uses of hydrogen.

x: Three are power or domestic uses: backup power, grid balancing and future heating. Methanol production is an industrial use.
t: Discriminate power uses from industrial uses.

x: Both are true: fuel cells are highly efficient, and green hydrogen can replace grey hydrogen in refineries.
t: Recall the uses of hydrogen.

x: All five are green-hydrogen uses: heavy vehicles, shipping, railways, long-duration energy storage and peak power.
t: Recall the uses of green hydrogen.

x: Hydrogen helps decarbonise cement, fertilisers, heavy transport and shipping, and the code pairs each sector with its own entry, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the hard-to-abate sectors.

x: Hydrogen suits hard-to-abate sectors such as steel, shipping and fertilisers, where direct electrification is difficult.
t: Recall why hydrogen targets hard-to-abate sectors.

x: Both are true: green hydrogen replaces fossil-based hydrogen and fuels, and so reduces India's dependence on imported oil and gas.
t: Recall the benefits of green hydrogen.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: a general global role does not by itself show why hydrogen is critical to India's 2070 net-zero goal.
t: Check whether R is specific enough to explain A.
